opening.headline: In the face of changes that are incompatible with 429 immediately after deployment, standards are established to determine which errors can be resent and which cannot.
body: When you attach an API to a service, you will encounter errors at some point. The problem is the response rather than the error itself. Code that immediately repeats a failed request makes the situation worse by placing more requests on already crowded servers.

In this class, we'll look at reading HTTP error codes for causes, retries and exponential backoff, and jitter to prevent retry flooding. Next, we cover the definition of idempotency, failures with unknown consequences, idempotent keys to safely resend requests with side effects such as payments, and protocols for handling API versions and deprecation notices.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain HTTP error codes and retry rules
You can distinguish between errors that can be retried and errors that cannot be retried.
This explains why we need to add jitter to the backoff.
You can distinguish between idempotent methods and non-idempotent methods, and determine whether a retry is possible in case of failure with unknown results.

screens.title: 429 and broken call immediately after deployment
screens.lead: Read along for the scenes from the day of the disability. It's a good idea to read it while thinking about what three problems you see in the log.

visual.alt: A scene showing a timetable showing a rapid increase in 429 responses after the distribution time and log fragments placed side by side.
labels: Change the appearance of the response

paragraphs: Immediately after deploying the new version, the API was flooded with 429 responses due to the influx of user requests. The service code was designed to immediately repeat failed requests, which made the situation worse by generating more requests.
Around the same time, the API's response appearance changed, making some calls incompatible. And I had one more worry. The problem is that the retry may have resulted in payment being executed twice.

The three issues may seem mixed, but each can be addressed with different tools: error classification, retry rules, and compatibility management. The questions in this lesson come together. Which errors can be resent, and which cannot?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is sending something back immediately when it fails always a sincere response? Answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Before organizing this confusing disorder into a classification system, let's first consider your own experience.

screens.title: Think about it: Was it okay to send it again?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a problem where the app keeps sending the same request during server maintenance or failure?
items.answer: It's common. Immediate retries after failures add load to already strained servers. So retries require a rule that increases the waiting time.

items.prompt: Have you ever heard of a payment or order being processed twice?
items.answer: Requests that do not receive a response do not know whether they were actually processed. If you just resend at this point, the same task may run twice. A device that prevents this problem is an idempotent key.

items.prompt: Think about the experience of your code breaking because an external API changed silently.
items.answer: If the caller is late in noticing that the response has changed, it becomes a hindrance. You can detect changes in advance by fixing the version and logging a header indicating that it will be discarded.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's first look at how to read the cause by the error code.

screens.title: What Causes Reading as HTTP Error Codes
screens.lead: Each row in the table shows the error code, cause, and whether to retry. Read from top to bottom to see where the errors that require you to fix your request differ from those that you can just wait for.

data.caption: Claude API error codes and responses
rows: 400 invalid_request_error
There is a problem with the format or content of your request. You will also receive this code when you reach a spending limit you set yourself.
Fix your request and resend it. If you repeat it over and over again, you will continue to fail.
401 authentication_error
There is a problem with your API key.
Check and correct the key. Retrying will not solve the problem.
402 billing_error
There's a problem with your payment information.
Correct your payment settings. Retrying will not solve the problem.
429 rate_limit_error
The speed limit has been reached.
Follow the retry-after header to wait and retry.
429 (monthly spending limit reached)
You have reached the monthly spending limit for your tier. There is no retry-after header, and error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached.
SDK automatic retries will also continue to fail until access is resumed. Request a higher tier or higher limit and don't repeat until then.
500 api_error
This is an internal server error.
Retries only a limited number of times with exponential backoff.
529 overloaded_error
It's a temporary overload.
Retries only a limited number of times with exponential backoff.
data.notes: The error response comes as a JSON structure containing type and message. Even if it is the same 429, the response varies depending on whether it is a speed limit or a spending limit, so check the presence or absence of the retry-after header.

screens.outro: Let's continue with the flow of how to retry some code.

screens.title: Retry and backoff, 429 header
screens.lead: Follow the retry decision flow step by step. Select the right arrow to turn on the branches one by one.

visual.alt: Flowchart for determining whether a retry is required when an error occurs and determining the waiting time.
labels: Is this a temporary failure? (Connection Error, 429, 5xx)

steps.title: 1. Select retry target
steps.body: Retry targets are transient failures such as connection errors, 429s, and 5xx. 4xx, where the request itself is incorrect, is not a target because the result is the same even if repeated as is.

steps.title: 2. If there is a retry-after, it follows.
steps.body: If there is a retry-after header in the 429 response, it waits for that amount of time and then sends it again. This value is provided directly by the server, so it is more accurate than my guess. The value of this header is either the number of seconds to wait or the time (date) at which it is okay to try again. Since it is the server's choice to include this header in the 429 response, a separate rule is needed to prepare for its absence.

steps.title: 3. Without exponential backoff
steps.body: Exponential backoff increases the waiting time to 1 second, 2 seconds, or 4 seconds to give the server room to recover. Put an upper limit on the number of times so it doesn't repeat infinitely. However, when there are many clients, this rule alone is not enough. The reason is explained in the following screen.

steps.title: 4. Basic operation of SDK
steps.body: The official SDK automatically retries transient failures such as connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx twice by default with exponential backoff, and follows the retry-after header if present. This behavior can be adjusted or turned off with `max_retries`. Before writing your own retry code, make sure it does not overlap with the SDK's behavior.

steps.title: 5. Nature of speed limits
steps.body: Rate limiting is token bucket-based. Capacity is not filled all at once at a fixed cycle, but continuously. So, if you wait a while, some capacity will come back.

steps.title: 6. 429 of spending limit is different
steps.body: A tier's monthly spending limit of 429 has no retry-after and will continue to fail until access is resumed at 00:00 UTC on the 1st of the following month. At this point, it makes no sense to iterate with a backoff and you should request a higher tier or higher limit. Since it is the same rate_limit_error type, it is distinguished from the rate limit by whether error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached.

screens.outro: Here's how to safely retry requests with side effects:

ext.title: RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes, 429 Too Many Requests (4)

screens.title: Why Backoff Isn't Alone: Retry Burst and Jitter
screens.lead: Use the slider to change how you set the retry interval. You can see that 1,000 clients receiving a 429 at the same moment change when they send the request again. Number of clients and times are assumed for illustrative purposes only.

visual.alt: A graph comparing the convergence or spread of requests arriving at the server by retry method on the time axis.
labels: Number of retry requests arriving at that moment
flock again at the same moment

stops.body: Assumption: The server is hit by a limit and returns 429 to 1,000 clients simultaneously. If everyone resends immediately after the failure, the server will receive another request of the same size as the one it just rejected. Servers that are already at their limit are hit with the same waves one after another, leaving no time to recover. This is the simplest form of the symptom: when you try again, it only gets worse.

Even if you change it so that all clients resend after 1 second, the situation is almost the same. There is only a gap of 1 second between waves, but the appearance of 1,000 waves arriving at the same moment is the same. If clients fail at the same time and wait with the same rule, the retry time is also the same.

Increasing the wait time to 1, 2, or 4 seconds increases the space between waves. However, since all clients start at the same time and follow the same rules, 1,000 will arrive all at once at 1, 3, and 7 seconds after the first failure. From the server's perspective, the influx of requests at the same moment is repeated with the intervals widening. This phenomenon of a large number of clients coming back at the same time is often called a thundering herd. The AWS Architecture Blog explains that retries from competing clients cluster together with backoff alone.

Jitter is adding randomness to latency. For example, if the wait limit for this turn is 4 seconds, it will not wait exactly 4 seconds, but a random value between 0 and 4 seconds. The value is different for each client, so retries are spread out over the time axis, and requests come in to the server at an almost constant rate. Simulations on the AWS Architecture Blog also report that adding jitter significantly reduces the total number of calls and finishes the job faster. The implementation cost is just one random number.

If the server informs you of the waiting time through retry-after, the rule is to follow that value. However, if all clients that received the same value retry at exactly the same time, they may be crowded again at that moment. So it is safer to spread out the retry times by adding some random delay after the given time. The server's instructions are followed, but my retries do not overlap with other clients.

screens.outro: Now that you've added jitter to the backoff, it's time to decide whether you can resend the request with side effects. First, let’s check the definition of idempotence.

screens.title: Idempotence is: a failure with unknown results and a request that can be resent.
screens.lead: Each row in the table shows what happens when one request method receives the same request twice. Read from top to bottom, focusing on whether the result on the server is the same even if you send each row twice.

data.caption: Idempotence and automatic retries by request method
columns: When the same request arrives twice
Can I send it again if I don't receive a response?
rows: GET (lookup)
It's idempotent. This is a safe method that does not change the server state.
Because it only searches, the results on the server are the same even if it is sent twice.
You can send it again without a separate device.
PUT (replace whole)
It's idempotent.
Even if you replace the same content twice, the final state is the same as if you replaced it once.
You can send it again without a separate device.
DELETE
It's idempotent.
In the second request, it has already been cleared, so the response may be different, but the final state is the same.
You can send it again without a separate device.
POST (Create/Execute)
It's not idempotent.
Each call can have new effects, such as creating an order or executing a payment.
It is only secure if there is a mechanism to prevent duplication, such as an idempotent key.
LLM message creation call (usually POST)
Each call costs money even if you don't change the data on the server. This is an explanation based on general principles.
The response content may vary, and input and output tokens are calculated separately for each call.
Your data will not be duplicated, but you may incur the same costs once more.
data.notes: Idempotent means that sending the same request multiple times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once. This does not mean that even the text of the response is the same. The reason this concept is important is because of failure without knowing the outcome. If the connection is lost or a timeout occurs after sending the request but before reading the response, the calling party will not know whether the server has processed the request. If it's an idempotent request, you can just resend it. The HTTP standard recommends that non-idempotent requests be automatically resent only when there is a means to prevent duplication or when it can be confirmed that they were not processed. Idempotent keys are one means of this.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the definition of idempotent, let's compare ways to secure non-idempotent requests using keys.

screens.title: Idempotent keys and API versions
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the presence or absence of a key changes the results in the same retry situation.

states.label: no key
states.body: I sent a payment request, but the connection was lost before I received a response. If the key is missing, the server sees and processes the retry request as a new request. If the first request was already successful, the same payment will be made twice. The root of the problem is that the server may have finished processing just because a response was not received. Even if you send a read request twice, the result will be the same, but if you send a request to change status, such as payment or order creation, the results will be different if you send it twice. When setting up retry rules, it is important to first distinguish this difference.

states.label: Has key
states.body: Stripe prevents duplicate execution of the same request with the `Idempotency-Key` header. API v1 stores the status code and body of the first request executed with the same key, and returns the saved response including a 500 error when sent again with the same key. If the parameters for the same key are different, an error occurs. The key can be up to 255 characters long, and keys that are older than 24 hours can be automatically cleaned up, and if you use the same key after being cleaned up, it will be processed as a new request. Therefore, the keys should be the same for the same task and different for different tasks. The retry code must retain the key created on the first attempt and use the same value on all retries. This way, no matter how many retries occur, the server treats them as one operation. Also decide in advance where to store the key. Even if the process is restarted, you should be able to retrieve the same key again.

screens.outro: The issue of changing versions is handled by a header that anchors the calling contract. Next we'll look at the standard way changes are announced.

screens.title: Version header, OpenAPI, deprecation notice header
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the role of the tools in managing compatibility. It is easier to understand if you divide the calling contract into two parts: those that fix it and those that announce changes.

tabs.label: anthropic-version
tabs.body: Anthropic specifies the API version with the header `anthropic-version`, an example in the documentation is `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`. Within the same version, Anthropic maintains existing input and output parameters. However, it is possible to add optional inputs, add output values, change the conditions for occurrence of a specific error type, or add new variants of enum-type output values ​​such as streaming events. Therefore, the client must structure it so that it does not break even if it encounters an unknown value.

tabs.label: beta header
tabs.body: Beta functions are used by putting the function name in the `anthropic-beta` header, and the exact name is written in the document for each function. Multiple functions can be placed in one header, separated by commas, and the SDK sends the header instead if you pass it as the `betas` parameter. Only requests with the header will use this feature, so it will be clear in your code which calls are using the beta.

tabs.label: OpenAPI
tabs.body: OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0 is a standard that describes HTTP APIs in machine-readable format. Once you have a specification, you can automatically create client code, documentation, and verifiers. If you keep the specification file by version, you can use it to compare before and after changes.

tabs.label: Deprecation header
tabs.body: RFC 9745 defines the `Deprecation` response header to indicate that a resource is scheduled for retirement. Decommissioning does not change the behavior of a resource; it is a signal to encourage clients to move away from that resource and not create new dependencies. If you see this header in the response, start preparing to replace that call. By logging response headers, you can detect compatibility changes in advance.

tabs.label: Sunset header
tabs.body: The `Sunset` header in RFC 8594 is intended to signal when a resource is expected to become unresponsive. While Deprecation tells you that something is due for decommissioning, Sunset tells you when it's going away. RFC 9745 stipulates that Sunset time must not be earlier than Deprecation time. By looking at both headers together, you can schedule replacements.

screens.outro: Now that we've covered all of the tools, let's move on to an illustrative example.

screens.title: Commentary: Payment API idempotency case
screens.lead: The instructor explains in a timeline how a payment request almost occurred twice. Select the right arrow to add events one by one.

visual.alt: A timeline of payment requests, disconnections, and retries in chronological order.
labels: Return the result of the first request

steps.title: 1. Payment request is sent
steps.body: The user presses the payment button, and the server calls the payment API. This call is a request that has the side effect of moving money.

steps.title: 2. It hangs up before a response comes.
steps.body: The network is disconnected before a response is received, so the result is unknown. Your payment may or may not have already been processed. There is no way for the calling party to distinguish between them.

steps.title: 3. If you retry without the key
steps.body: If you resend the same request without the key, the server will treat it as a new request. If the first request was successful, the same payment will be made twice. This is the identity of the anxiety I felt when I first became disabled.

steps.title: 4. If you retry with the same key
steps.body: If you send again to the same `Idempotency-Key`, the server will return the result of the first request. Payment only happens once, and the calling party can retry with confidence.

steps.title: 5. What are keys made of?
steps.body: The method of creating the key is determined by the calling party. Stripe recommends a string that is random enough to avoid collisions, such as V4 UUID, and advises against using sensitive information such as email as the key. The key is to create and store one key per task and reuse that value on each retry. If you create a new key for each retry, the server will see it as a different request and the protection will be lost.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the principle, let's expand it to other errors and create a retry classification table.

screens.title: Commentary: Classification table for errors that can and cannot be retried
screens.lead: The instructor classifies each type of error line by line and explains the reason for the judgment. Select the right arrow to advance to the next row.

steps.title: 400, 401, 402: Do not retry
steps.body: Until you correct your request or account, the results will be the same no matter how many times you send it. These errors should be corrected at the cause rather than repeated immediately. Repetition only adds load.

steps.title: 429 (rate limit): wait and retry
steps.body: It waits for the retry-after header, and if not, retries with an exponential backoff to widen the interval. Rate limiting is lifted by waiting as capacity is filled continuously.

steps.title: 429 (Spending Limit): Cannot be resolved by waiting.
steps.body: There is no retry-after and access will continue to fail until restored. You may need to increase the limit or change the settings. Even for the same 429, the speed limit and spending limit correspond directly to each other.

steps.title: 500, 529: Retry limited number of times
steps.body: Server internal errors and transient overloads are retried with exponential backoff. However, place an upper limit on the number of times to prevent repetition.

steps.title: Calls with side effects only occur when the key is present
steps.body: Even if the error is retryable, calls with side effects, such as payments, can only be safely retried if there is an idempotent key. If you don't have the key, consider checking the results by querying them first. If you create a classification table like this, even if you encounter a new error, you can decide on a response based on the same criteria. It is recommended that the classification table be reflected in the code's retry policy and failure response documentation. When everyone on the team shares the same standards, the timing of failures can be determined faster.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Retry is done after classification.
screens.lead: Let's go back to the initial failure scene and summarize the criteria for error handling once and for all.

paragraphs: The first question was which errors can be resent and which cannot. 4xx are errors that require the request to be fixed, while 429, 500, and 529 are things to wait for and retry. Even for the same 429, the response varies depending on whether it is a speed limit or a spending limit.

Retries are spaced out with exponential backoff, distributed with jitter, and follow the retry-after if there is one. For requests with side effects, such as payments, an idempotent key is attached to prevent duplicate execution. Compatibility is fixed with the version header, and changes are detected in advance with the OpenAPI specification and Deprecation header.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Immediate retries after failure place a greater load on the server. Sort, wait, prevent duplication, and send again.

glossary.def: Exponential backoff is a method of increasing the retry interval such as 1 second, 2 seconds, or 4 seconds, and jitter is adding randomness to the waiting time to distribute the retry times of multiple clients.
This is a response header that tells you how soon to try again.

Idempotence means that even if you send the same request multiple times, the effect remaining on the server is the same as sending it once. An idempotent key is an identifier that can be attached to a non-idempotent request to ensure that a request with the same key is executed only once.
Request header that pins the API contract version.
Response header indicating that the resource is scheduled for retirement. Defined in RFC 9745.
This is a specification that describes the HTTP API in a machine-readable manner.

misconceptions.myth: All errors are resolved by retrying.
misconceptions.fact: 400 request errors will continue to fail unless you fix the request. Retries are only for transient failures such as connection errors, 429, and 5xx.

misconceptions.myth: 429 always resolves if you wait for a while.
misconceptions.fact: Rate limits 429 are released by waiting, but spend limit 429s have no retry-after and will continue to fail until access is restored.

misconceptions.myth: An idempotent key can be any value.
misconceptions.fact: You must create one key per task and reuse it for each retry. If a new key is created for each retry, the duplication prevention effect is lost, and an error occurs if the same key has different parameters. Keys must be unique enough to avoid collisions and must not contain sensitive information.

misconceptions.myth: Just adding an exponential backoff can prevent retry flooding.
misconceptions.fact: If all clients wait according to the same rules, they will flock again at the same moment, leaving a wide gap between them. There should be jitter to add randomness to the latency to spread out retries.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: 4xx are errors that require the request to be fixed, while 429, 500, and 529 are things to wait for and retry.
Retries are spaced with exponential backoff, distributed with jitter, and follow the retry-after header if present.

Requests that are not idempotent methods cannot be determined whether they will be processed when a response is not received, so duplicate execution of requests such as payment is prevented with an idempotent key.
Anthropic-version headers and beta headers fix the calling contract and prepare it for changes.
The OpenAPI specification and Deprecation header (RFC 9745) make compatibility changes machine-readable.

checks.q: The 429 response keeps coming, but there is no retry-after header, and it does not recover even if I wait. What is the most likely cause and response?
options: You've reached your tier's monthly spending limit and need to request a higher limit or tier.
Since it is blocked by the speed limit, it repeats at the same interval until retry-after comes.
Since the server is overloaded (529), the number of requests is doubled to process them.
This is an API key issue (401) and will be resolved soon by reissuing the key.
checks.explain: 429s that hit your tier's monthly spending limit have no retry-after and will continue to fail until access is resumed, so the solution is to request a higher limit or tier rather than repeat.

wrong.1: The 429 in the speed limit usually comes with a retry-after, and the 429 in the spending limit does not.
wrong.2: Increasing requests makes things worse, and 529 is another status code.
wrong.3: The key issue is 401 authentication_error, which is distinct from 429.

checks.q: Thousands of clients receive 429 at the same moment, and they all retry with exponential backoff at 1, 2, or 4 second intervals. How to reduce the problem of repeated requests at the same moment?
options: Add randomness (jitter) to the retry waiting time to distribute the retry time.
Increase the interval for all clients by further increasing the backoff stage to 8 seconds and 16 seconds.
Removes the upper limit on the number of retries and continues sending until success.
Ignore the retry-after header and resend as soon as possible
checks.explain: Backoff only widens the gap, and if all clients move at the same time and with the same rules, retries are concentrated at the same moment. Adding randomness to the wait time spreads the retries across the time base.

wrong.1: Just increase the spacing and everyone will still arrive at the same time because they all start at the same time and follow the same rules.
wrong.2: Removing the upper limit will only make the load last longer.
wrong.3: If you ignore the waiting time notified by the server, you will end up placing more requests on an already crowded server.
